source.title: Essentialism
source.attribution: A summary of Essentialism by Greg McKeown (2014). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright.

cards.title: Do fewer things, but do them much better
cards.body:
McKeown's core idea is that trying to do everything spreads your effort so thin that nothing gets real progress. Essentialism is the deliberate habit of figuring out what truly matters and putting your energy there, while letting the rest go.

He warns that if you don't choose your priorities, other people will choose them for you, filling your days with their requests. Being selective is not laziness; it is how you make a meaningful contribution instead of a scattered one.
cards.apply_it: Write down the three things that matter most to you this month. Cross off one commitment that doesn't serve any of them.

quiz.question: What is the core idea of essentialism?
options: Choose what matters most and pursue it deliberately
Do as much as possible
Avoid all hard work
Say yes to every opportunity
quiz.explanation: It is the disciplined pursuit of fewer, more important things.

cards.title: Every yes carries a trade-off, so choose it on purpose
cards.body:
McKeown argues that trade-offs are unavoidable. Time and energy are limited, so agreeing to one thing always means giving up another. Many people pretend otherwise and try to have it all, which leads to overcommitment and mediocre results.

Instead of asking how to fit everything in, ask which option you most want and what you are willing to give up for it. Facing the trade-off openly turns a stressful juggling act into a clear decision.
cards.apply_it: For your next request, ask yourself: if I say yes to this, what am I saying no to?

quiz.question: How does McKeown suggest handling trade-offs?
options: Avoid them by working harder
Pretend they don't exist
Let others decide
Accept them and choose deliberately what to give up
quiz.explanation: Trade-offs are a fact of life, so the essentialist makes them consciously.

cards.title: If it isn't a clear yes, treat it as a no
cards.body:
When evaluating an opportunity, McKeown suggests setting a high bar. Pick the single most important criterion and score the option against it. If it doesn't score strongly, perhaps around 90 out of 100, decline it.

The reasoning is that lukewarm options quietly fill your calendar and crowd out the rare opportunities that really matter. Being extremely selective feels uncomfortable at first, but it keeps room open for the things you would be genuinely excited about.
cards.apply_it: Rate a current invitation or project from 0 to 100 on your top criterion. If it scores below 90, plan how to decline.

quiz.question: What does McKeown suggest doing with an opportunity that is merely 'fine'?
options: Accept it to be safe
Delegate it automatically
Decline it unless it's a clear yes
Postpone it indefinitely
quiz.explanation: A strict threshold keeps space for the opportunities that truly matter.

cards.title: Say no kindly by separating the decision from the person
cards.body:
Many people say yes because refusing feels rude. McKeown points out that declining a request is not the same as rejecting the person who asked. You can respect the relationship and still turn down the task.

He suggests practical ways to do it well: a warm but clear refusal, a pause before answering, offering something smaller you can do, or pointing to someone better placed to help. People often respect a graceful no more than a grudging yes that you later fail to deliver.
cards.apply_it: Draft a short, friendly template for saying no that you can reuse, and use it the next time you need it.

quiz.question: What is McKeown's key insight about saying no?
options: Always explain at length
Refusing a request is not rejecting the person
Never say no to your boss
Say no only by email
quiz.explanation: Separating the decision from the relationship makes it easier to decline gracefully.

cards.title: Build in a buffer because things take longer than planned
cards.body:
McKeown notes that people routinely underestimate how long tasks will take. Plans built with no slack collapse at the first delay, forcing rushed work and stress.

His remedy is to add extra time to estimates, often around half again as much, and to prepare for likely setbacks in advance. A buffer is not wasted time; it is what lets you deliver calmly on what matters instead of constantly firefighting.
cards.apply_it: Take your next deadline estimate and add 50% to it before you commit to anyone.

quiz.question: Why does McKeown recommend adding buffers?
options: Because we tend to underestimate how long things take
To work less
To impress clients
Because deadlines don't matter
quiz.explanation: Estimates tend to be too optimistic, so slack protects your important work.

cards.title: You always keep the power to choose what you take on
cards.body:
McKeown argues that many overloaded people slowly start to feel they have no choice: the boss decides, the family decides, the schedule decides. He links this to learned helplessness, where people stop trying because they believe their actions don't matter.

His response is that the ability to choose can be ignored or given away, but never fully taken from you. Recognising this is the first step of essentialism. Instead of saying 'I have to', you start asking 'What do I choose to do here?'
cards.apply_it: Notice the next time you say 'I have to'. Rephrase it as 'I choose to' or 'I choose not to' and see how it feels.

quiz.question: What does McKeown say about our ability to choose?
options: Only senior managers have real choice
Choice is an illusion
Choosing less makes us weaker
We can forget or give it away, but it is never fully taken from us
quiz.explanation: He sees choice as something we can neglect but never completely lose, which is the root of essentialism.

cards.title: Explore widely first, so you can commit deeply to the few that matter
cards.body:
It might seem that an essentialist would explore less, but McKeown argues the opposite. Because essentialists plan to commit to only a few things, they take more time at the start to look at many options, listen, debate and think before deciding.

The reasoning is that most opportunities are noise and only a few are worth a big investment. Careful exploration up front is how you tell them apart, so that when you do say yes, you can go all in.
cards.apply_it: Before your next big commitment, list at least five options and spend some time comparing them before choosing one.

quiz.question: Why does McKeown say essentialists explore more options, not fewer?
options: Because they enjoy being busy
Because they never commit to anything
Because they will commit to only a few, so they need to choose well
Because exploring is a way to avoid decisions
quiz.explanation: Exploring widely helps separate the vital few from the trivial many before committing deeply.

cards.title: Success can quietly pull you away from what made you successful
cards.body:
McKeown describes a pattern he calls the paradox of success. When you have a clear purpose, you do good work and succeed. Success brings more requests and opportunities. Saying yes to them spreads your effort thinly, and soon you lose the clarity that made you successful in the first place.

He warns that this applies to individuals and organisations alike. The fix is to notice the pattern and deliberately protect your focus as opportunities grow, rather than treating every new option as something you should accept.
cards.apply_it: Think of something you became known for. List the new commitments it brought, and mark which ones are diluting your main work.

quiz.question: What is the 'paradox of success' McKeown describes?
options: Successful people never get new opportunities
Success brings so many options that it can undermine the focus that caused it
Success always leads to more clarity
Failing is better than succeeding
quiz.explanation: Clarity leads to success, which brings options, which spread effort and erode clarity.

cards.title: Block out time just to think
cards.body:
McKeown argues that you cannot choose what is essential if you never stop to think. Busy people fill every gap, so there's no room left to reflect on what truly matters.

He gives examples of leaders who protect thinking time, including a chief executive who blocked out two hours a day with nothing scheduled, and Bill Gates's habit of taking a week away to read and reflect. Even a short, regular slot of quiet thinking can help you see your priorities more clearly.
cards.apply_it: Schedule a 30-minute meeting with yourself this week with no agenda except thinking about your priorities. Keep your phone away.

quiz.question: Why does McKeown recommend blocking time just to think?
options: You can't discern what's essential without space to reflect
It looks impressive to others
It replaces the need to make decisions
Thinking time is only for executives
quiz.explanation: Without space to think, you can't separate the essential from the trivial.

cards.title: Look for the real story, like a good journalist
cards.body:
McKeown tells a story from Nora Ephron's school days: a teacher asked students to write the lead of a news story about a staff event, and then pointed out that the real news was that there would be no school that day. The lesson was to look past the details to what actually matters.

He suggests applying this to life and work. In meetings, conversations and projects, ask what the essential point is. Filtering out noise to find the true issue helps you respond to what matters instead of what is loudest.
cards.apply_it: After your next meeting, write down in one sentence the most important thing that came out of it.

quiz.question: What does the 'journalist' lesson in Essentialism teach?
options: Report every detail in order
Always write long reports
Trust headlines without checking
Look past the details to find what really matters
quiz.explanation: Like a good journalist, you find the lead: the essential point behind the details.

cards.title: Play isn't a waste of time; it helps you think
cards.body:
McKeown argues that adults often treat play as trivial, something to squeeze in after real work is done. Drawing on researchers who study play, he suggests that activities done purely for enjoyment help reduce stress, spark creativity and open the mind to new possibilities.

For an essentialist, play is part of how you explore options and stay fresh enough to spot what matters. A little time spent doing something just for fun can make you sharper at the things you care about most.
cards.apply_it: Think of something you loved doing as a child. Find a small way to do a version of it this week.

quiz.question: How does McKeown view play?
options: As a waste of productive time
As only suitable for children
As something that helps creativity and exploration
As a reward to be earned only after all work is done
quiz.explanation: He sees play as a way to reduce stress, open the mind and explore, not as a distraction.

cards.title: Protect your sleep, because you are your main asset
cards.body:
McKeown argues that your mind and body are the main tools you bring to everything that matters, so wearing them down is a poor trade. Many ambitious people treat cutting back on sleep as a badge of commitment, but he sees it as damaging the very abilities you need to do your best work.

He encourages treating rest as a priority rather than a weakness. Being well rested helps you think clearly, make better choices and notice which activities truly deserve your energy.
cards.apply_it: Decide on a consistent time to go to bed this week, and set a reminder an hour before to start winding down.

quiz.question: Why does McKeown treat sleep as a priority?
options: Because sleeping less proves commitment
Because your mind and body are the main asset you use for everything
Because rest only matters for athletes
Because work is unimportant
quiz.explanation: He says protecting the asset, you, through sleep keeps you able to think and choose well.

cards.title: Turn vague goals into a clear, concrete intent
cards.body:
McKeown observes that many teams and people work from mission statements so general they guide nothing, or from quarterly targets so narrow they inspire no one. He suggests an essential intent: a goal that is both inspiring and concrete, meaningful and measurable.

A good essential intent makes many later decisions easy, because you can check each option against it. He likens it to making one decision that settles a thousand others. If you can't tell when you've achieved it, it is probably too vague.
cards.apply_it: Rewrite one of your goals so it is specific enough that you'd know when you've reached it, but still matters to you.

quiz.question: What two qualities should an 'essential intent' have?
options: Inspiring and concrete
Vague and flexible
Short-term and easy
Secret and complicated
quiz.explanation: An essential intent is meaningful and measurable, so it guides many later decisions.

cards.title: Don't keep investing in something just because you've already invested
cards.body:
McKeown discusses the sunk-cost bias: the tendency to keep putting time, money or effort into a project because of what you've already spent, even when it's clearly not working. The more we've invested, the harder it is to walk away.

He encourages accepting that past costs are gone whatever you do next. The question is only whether future investment makes sense. Admitting a mistake can feel painful, but it frees you to put your resources somewhere better.
cards.apply_it: Name one project, purchase or commitment you're keeping mainly because of what you've already put in. Ask: would I start this today?

quiz.question: What is the sunk-cost bias?
options: Refusing to spend money on anything new
Saving money for emergencies
Always quitting projects too early
Continuing to invest because of what you've already spent, even when it isn't working
quiz.explanation: Past costs are gone; the right question is whether future investment is worthwhile.

cards.title: Rebuild your commitments from zero instead of just trimming them
cards.body:
McKeown warns about the status quo bias: we keep doing things simply because we've always done them. He borrows the idea of zero-based budgeting from accounting, where each expense must be justified from scratch rather than starting from last year's figure.

Applied to your time, this means imagining you have no commitments at all, then asking which ones you would add back today. Anything that wouldn't earn its place in a fresh plan is a candidate to drop.
cards.apply_it: List your regular commitments. Pretend they all disappeared, and circle only the ones you would choose again today.

quiz.question: What does applying zero-based budgeting to your time involve?
options: Keeping everything you did last year
Adding new commitments every month
Justifying each commitment from scratch instead of keeping it by default
Letting others choose your commitments
quiz.explanation: Starting from zero fights the status quo bias by making each commitment earn its place.

cards.title: Test quietly dropping a task to see if anyone notices
cards.body:
McKeown suggests what he calls a reverse pilot. Instead of testing a new initiative, you test removing an existing one. Stop producing a report, skip a routine meeting or cut back a recurring task, and observe whether it makes any difference.

Often nobody notices or misses it, which tells you the activity was not essential. If it turns out to matter, you can bring it back. This makes it easier to cut work safely without a big debate.
cards.apply_it: Pick one recurring task you suspect adds little value. Pause it for two weeks and see if anyone asks about it.

quiz.question: What is a 'reverse pilot' in Essentialism?
options: Trying a new product before launch
Testing whether removing an activity makes any difference
Doing a task twice to check it
Asking a colleague to take over your work
quiz.explanation: You temporarily remove an activity to see if it is missed; if not, it may be non-essential.

cards.title: Ask what you would pay for something if you didn't already own it
cards.body:
McKeown describes the endowment effect: people tend to value things more simply because they own them. The same applies to commitments, roles and projects; once they are ours, we struggle to let go even when they no longer serve us.

His counter is to imagine you don't own it yet. If I didn't already have this, how much would I pay to get it? If I weren't already involved in this project, how hard would I work to join it? Answering honestly can make letting go much easier.
cards.apply_it: Choose one item or commitment you're attached to. Ask yourself what you would pay or give to get it if you didn't have it.

quiz.question: How does McKeown suggest countering the endowment effect?
options: Imagine you don't own it yet and ask how much you'd pay for it
Buy more things to compare
Keep everything just in case
Ask a salesperson for advice
quiz.explanation: Pretending you don't yet own something helps you judge its real value to you.

cards.title: Edit your life the way a good editor edits a book
cards.body:
McKeown compares essentialism to the work of a skilled film or book editor. Good editing is mostly invisible: it cuts what isn't needed, condenses what remains so it says more with less, and corrects course when things drift.

He also notes that a good editor knows when to hold back and change less. Applied to your schedule or a project, this means regularly removing excess, tightening what's left, and resisting the urge to keep adding. The result is cleaner, clearer work and a calmer life.
cards.apply_it: Look at tomorrow's plan and cut one item completely, then shorten another so it takes less time.

quiz.question: Which actions does McKeown associate with editing your life?
options: Adding, expanding and repeating
Delaying, avoiding and forgetting
Copying, sharing and posting
Cutting, condensing and correcting
quiz.explanation: Like an editor, you cut what's unneeded, condense what's left and correct course.

cards.title: Clear boundaries free you rather than restrict you
cards.body:
McKeown argues that boundaries are not walls that shut people out; they are what let you protect time and energy for what matters. Without them, other people's priorities can slowly take over your days.

He points out that some people will try to make their problems your problems. Setting limits in advance, and helping others solve their own problems instead of taking them on yourself, keeps you available for your essential work and can even help others grow in responsibility.
cards.apply_it: Think of one request you regularly accept that isn't really your job. Decide on a polite limit you'll state next time it comes up.

quiz.question: How does McKeown see boundaries?
options: As selfish and unkind
As something only managers need
As freeing, because they protect your time for what matters
As a way to avoid all teamwork
quiz.explanation: Boundaries protect your energy for what's essential and stop others' problems becoming yours.

cards.title: Remove the biggest obstacle instead of pushing harder
cards.body:
McKeown borrows an idea from Eliyahu Goldratt's business novel The Goal: in any process, the slowest step limits the whole. In the novel, a group hike moves only as fast as its slowest walker, so the leader reorganises the group around him.

The lesson is that adding effort everywhere achieves little if one constraint is holding everything back. Instead, identify what is slowing progress most on your essential goal, and focus on removing that obstacle. Subtracting a barrier often achieves more than adding new activity.
cards.apply_it: For your most important goal, write down the single biggest thing slowing it down. Plan one step this week to reduce it.

quiz.question: What lesson does McKeown take from The Goal?
options: Make everyone work faster at the same time
Find and remove the biggest constraint that slows everything down
Add more steps to the process
Ignore slow team members
quiz.explanation: The slowest part of a system limits the whole, so removing that obstacle has the biggest effect.

cards.title: Small, visible wins build momentum
cards.body:
McKeown argues that essentialists don't try to do everything with a grand burst of effort. They start small and celebrate progress, because seeing steady wins is one of the most powerful motivators there is.

He suggests focusing on the minimum viable progress: the smallest useful step towards your goal. Rewarding and noticing these steps, rather than waiting for a big final result, helps the essential activity become easier and more natural over time.
cards.apply_it: Define the smallest meaningful step on an important goal. Do it today and mark it somewhere you'll see it.

quiz.question: What does McKeown mean by 'minimum viable progress'?
options: The smallest useful step that moves an important goal forward
Doing the least work possible to avoid blame
Waiting for the perfect moment to begin
Finishing a project in one big push
quiz.explanation: Small useful steps, noticed and celebrated, create momentum on what matters.

cards.title: Start important work early, even for just ten minutes
cards.body:
McKeown recommends what he calls minimal viable preparation. As soon as you learn about a project or deadline, spend a few minutes on it right away: jot down ideas, create a draft outline or list the first steps.

This small early start prevents the last-minute rush that leads to stress and poor work. It also gives your mind time to keep working on the problem in the background, so when you come back to it, you're further along than you'd expect.
cards.apply_it: Next time you're given a task with a deadline, spend ten minutes on it the same day, even if it's just an outline.

quiz.question: What is McKeown's 'minimal viable preparation'?
options: Preparing only the night before
Delegating every task immediately
Waiting until you feel inspired
Spending a little time on a task as soon as it arrives
quiz.explanation: An early, small start avoids last-minute rushing and lets ideas develop over time.

cards.title: Design routines that make the essential happen automatically
cards.body:
McKeown argues that relying on fresh effort and discipline each day is tiring. A good routine makes the essential activity the default, so you do it without having to decide.

He uses the example of the swimmer Michael Phelps, whose coach built a detailed pre-race routine that he followed every time, so his mind and body were ready without extra thought. McKeown suggests setting up your own routines around your most important work, linking them to clear cues so they run smoothly.
cards.apply_it: Choose your most important daily activity. Attach it to a fixed time or cue so it happens without debate.

quiz.question: Why does McKeown value routines?
options: They make every day exciting and unpredictable
They replace the need for goals
They make essential work the default, without constant decisions
They are only useful for athletes
quiz.explanation: Routines turn the essential into an automatic habit, reducing reliance on willpower.

cards.title: Keep asking: what's important now?
cards.body:
McKeown shares a question used by a rugby coach to keep his players present in the moment: what's important now? Instead of dwelling on past mistakes or worrying about the future, the team focused on the next essential action.

McKeown suggests this question for daily life too. When you feel overwhelmed by many demands, pause, breathe and ask what matters most right now. Then give that one thing your attention before moving on to the next.
cards.apply_it: Write 'What's important now?' on a sticky note and place it where you'll see it during busy moments.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of asking 'What's important now?'
options: To plan the next five years
To focus on the most essential action in the present moment
To review all past mistakes
To make a list of everything you could do
quiz.explanation: The question pulls attention away from past and future worries to the next essential action.

cards.title: You can do two things at once, but not focus on two things at once
cards.body:
McKeown makes a distinction between multitasking and what he calls multi-focusing. We can physically do more than one thing at a time, like walking while chatting. What we can't do well is concentrate on two important things at the same moment.

The problem isn't doing several activities; it's splitting attention between several priorities. He encourages giving your full focus to one essential thing at a time, especially when it is demanding, rather than trying to think hard about several things simultaneously.
cards.apply_it: In your next important conversation or task, put everything else away and notice how it feels to focus on just one thing.

quiz.question: What distinction does McKeown draw?
options: Doing several activities is possible; focusing on several priorities is not
Multitasking is always bad and single-tasking is always good
Focusing on many things is a skill everyone should learn
There is no difference between the two
quiz.explanation: The real problem is multi-focusing, splitting attention among several important things.

cards.title: There can only really be one top priority
cards.body:
McKeown points out that the word 'priority' entered English in the singular, meaning the very first or prior thing. Only much later did people start talking about 'priorities' in the plural, as if many things could all come first.

He uses this history to make a point: when everything is a priority, nothing is. Being willing to name one thing as most important at any given time forces honest choices and makes it clear where your energy should go.
cards.apply_it: Of everything on your list this week, choose the single top priority and write it at the very top of the page.

quiz.question: What point does McKeown make about the word 'priority'?
options: It has always been used in the plural
It means anything that is urgent
It refers only to business goals
It originally meant one thing, showing only one thing can come first
quiz.explanation: The word was originally singular, a reminder that if everything is a priority, nothing is.

cards.title: Keep a short journal to spot what really matters over time
cards.body:
McKeown recommends keeping a simple journal. He suggests writing less than you feel like writing, so the habit stays easy, perhaps just a few lines a day.

The value comes later. When you read back over your entries every few months, you start to notice patterns: what drained you, what energised you, which small details turned out to matter. It is a way of becoming the journalist of your own life, seeing trends you would miss day to day.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, write three short lines about your day. Set a reminder to reread your entries in three months.

quiz.question: What does McKeown suggest about journal writing?
options: Write long entries and never reread them
Only write when something dramatic happens
Write less than you feel like and review it every few months
Share every entry publicly
quiz.explanation: Brief entries keep the habit going, and periodic review reveals patterns.

cards.title: Teams without a clear purpose drift into politics and confusion
cards.body:
McKeown observes that when a team doesn't know what it is really trying to achieve, people fill the gap with their own agendas. Energy goes into competing for attention and influence rather than into meaningful work, or people simply spread their effort across too many things.

He argues that clarity of purpose is one of the most powerful things a leader can provide. When everyone understands the essential intent, decisions become easier, effort lines up, and people feel more motivated because they can see how their work matters.
cards.apply_it: Ask your team or family: what is the one thing we are really trying to achieve? Compare the answers.

quiz.question: What tends to happen in a team without a clear purpose, according to McKeown?
options: Everyone automatically works harder
People pursue their own agendas and effort gets scattered
The team becomes more creative
Nothing changes at all
quiz.explanation: Without clear purpose, politics and scattered effort fill the gap.

cards.title: Aim for your highest point of contribution
cards.body:
McKeown suggests that the guiding question for an essentialist is not how to do everything, but where you can make your highest point of contribution. That means the place where your particular skills and passions can do the most good for what matters.

With that in mind, you can turn down tasks that others could do as well as you, or that add little value, and invest your energy where it makes the biggest difference. It turns choosing less into a way of giving more.
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself: what could I do at work or at home that adds the most value and that few others could do as well? Write your answer down.

quiz.question: What is McKeown's guiding question for choosing where to put effort?
options: Where can I make my highest point of contribution?
How can I fit more tasks into my day?
What do other people expect of me?
What is easiest to finish today?
quiz.explanation: He encourages directing energy where your skills create the most value for what matters.

cards.title: Make essentialism a way of life, not an occasional tactic
cards.body:
McKeown distinguishes between people who use essentialist ideas now and then, perhaps when overwhelmed, and those who adopt them as part of who they are. Occasional decluttering helps, but the busyness creeps back.

He argues that the real benefits come when choosing less but better becomes your default mindset. Over time, this leads to more clarity, more control over your choices and more joy in the things you do commit to.
cards.apply_it: Pick one essentialist habit from the book, such as pausing before saying yes, and practise it every day for a week.

quiz.question: What does McKeown say brings the real benefits of essentialism?
options: Using it only when you feel overwhelmed
Trying it once a year
Reading about it without acting
Making it your ongoing way of life
quiz.explanation: Living it consistently, rather than occasionally, brings lasting clarity and control.
